text:
The story of the lighthouse, as it continues, finds itself woven into the fabric of a larger, quieter landscape. The tower, once a solitary sentinel against the sky, becomes a reference point in the minds of those who have spent their lives along the shore. The memory of the tin of tea, left on the shelf above the sink, grows increasingly significant. It is no longer just a faded label, but a small, tangible reminder of the simple acts of daily life that once sustained the keeper and the people who used the harbour.

As the seasons change, the tower begins to feel more like a piece of the earth itself. The rust on the iron gallery has deepened, and the shadow of the tower on the water seems to stretch longer each evening. This is a lesson in patience, a reminder that time moves slowly over a place that has been left to stand. The tide, once a constant companion, now seems to have a rhythm that can be felt in the small movements of the water near the base of the tower.

The story also takes in the people who have visited the tower over the years. There are the fishermen who come to cast their nets, the sailors who pass by in small boats, and the tourists who come to photograph the tower against the sky
